scenes.heading: Trailhead
scenes.subtitle: Crowd-sourced trail conditions
scenes.narration: Trailhead is a plan for crowd-sourced trail conditions. Hikers report mud, snow, fallen trees and closures from their phones, and everyone else sees a fresh, map-based view before they leave home.

scenes.heading: The problem and the goals
items: Today this lives in scattered Facebook groups, usually days old
Post a report in under 30 seconds, even offline
Reports older than 7 days are marked stale
Every report links to a known trail
scenes.narration: Today this information lives in scattered Facebook groups and is usually days old. The goals: post a report in under thirty seconds, even offline, mark reports older than seven days as stale, and tie every report to a known trail.

scenes.heading: Decisions and assumptions

items.label: A web app, not native apps
items.text: One codebase, no app-store review, offline support through a service worker.

items.label: Weak signal
items.text: Most reports are made at the trailhead or on the trail, often with weak or no signal.

items.label: Freshness at read time
items.text: Computed when a report is read, so nothing needs a nightly job.

scenes.narration: Two decisions shape everything. Start as a mobile web app, not native apps. And compute freshness when a report is read, so no nightly job is needed. The plan assumes most reports happen with weak or no signal.

scenes.heading: How a report travels
scenes.narration: A report starts in the app and waits in a queue on the phone until there is a connection. It is then posted to the API and stored in Postgres, next to trails imported from OpenStreetMap. The map reads from there.

scenes.heading: Four phases
scenes.narration: The work runs in four phases. Foundations sets up the project, the database and the trail catalogue. Reporting adds the form and offline sync. Then the map and freshness, and finally launch.

scenes.heading: Everything hangs off the trail catalogue
scenes.narration: Trails are imported from OpenStreetMap into one table, keyed by their OSM relation id. Every report points at one of them.

scenes.heading: Where the offline code lives
scenes.narration: Offline support comes from a service worker that caches the app shell, and a queue in IndexedDB that holds drafts until the connection returns.

scenes.heading: Risks and open questions

items.label: Photo privacy
items.text: Photos may reveal other hikers' faces.

items.label: Inconsistent names
items.text: OSM trail names differ across regions.

items.label: Spam
items.text: Fake reports before moderation tools exist.

items.label: Expire or fade?
items.text: Should reports expire completely, or only fade?

items.label: Accounts?
items.text: Are accounts needed, or is a device id enough for v1?

scenes.narration: Three risks stand out: photos that reveal other hikers, inconsistent trail names, and spam before moderation exists. Two questions are still open: whether reports should expire or only fade, and whether v1 needs accounts.

scenes.heading: What success looks like
items: 200 weekly active reporters across at least 3 regions
Posting a report takes under 30 seconds
scenes.narration: Launch is a success at two hundred weekly active reporters across at least three regions, with reports under a day old, and a post that takes under thirty seconds.
